summary: 2 Timothy has the form of a farewell letter. Paul appears imprisoned in Rome, abandoned by many and sure that death is approaching: “I am already being poured out like a drink offering” (4:6). He writes to Timothy, whom he calls “my beloved child,” to encourage him not to be ashamed of the gospel, to endure hardship like a soldier, to pass the teaching on to faithful people and to remain in the Scriptures he has known since childhood, at a time of deceiving teachers. The last chapter, with the review of his own life and a series of requests and news about co-workers, is one of the most personal passages attributed to Paul.
name: The title Pros Timotheon B, “Second to Timothy,” comes from the recipient, called “my beloved child” (1:2); the number distinguishes it from the first letter to him. With 1 Timothy and Titus, it forms the group of the “Pastoral Epistles.”
facts: 16th book of the New Testament; 11th of the Pauline letters, in canonical order
personal letter of exhortation, in a farewell tone (pastoral letter)

structure.title: Not being ashamed
structure.text: Paul recalls Timothy's faith, inherited from his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, asks him to fan into flame the gift of God and not to be ashamed of the prisoner; he contrasts those who deserted him in Asia with Onesiphorus, who searched for him in Rome.

structure.title: Steadfastness in service
structure.text: Images of the soldier, the athlete and the farmer; a saying about dying and living with Christ; avoiding useless quarrels, like those of Hymenaeus and Philetus, and correcting with gentleness.

structure.title: Difficult times and the Scriptures
structure.text: A portrait of the wicked in the last days; Paul's example in persecutions; the Scriptures, inspired by God and useful for teaching and correction.

structure.title: Final charge and news
structure.text: “Preach the word”; Paul sees his own life coming to an end; asks Timothy to come before winter, to bring Mark, the cloak and the parchments, and tells how he was left alone at his first defense.

people.name: Paul

people.name: Lois and Eunice
people.note: Timothy's grandmother and mother, remembered for their sincere faith (1:5)

writing.tradition: Tradition considers 2 Timothy Paul's last letter, written in Rome during a second imprisonment, shortly before his death under Nero, c. 64–67. Eusebius, in the 4th century, already understood the “first defense” of 4:16 as a sign that Paul had been released once and later arrested again.
writing.academic: With 1 Timothy and Titus, 2 Timothy forms the group of the Pastoral Epistles, which most critical scholars attribute to a disciple of Paul writing in his name between c. 90 and 120, because of their own vocabulary and style, their concern for the faithful transmission of teaching and the difficulty of fitting the letters into Paul's life. 2 Timothy, however, is often treated separately: it is the most personal of the three, full of names, requests and concrete details, such as the cloak left in Troas (4:13). For this reason some researchers who doubt 1 Timothy and Titus accept that 2 Timothy is by Paul or preserves authentic notes of his, especially in chapter 4; others see these details as a device to bring the figure of the apostle to life; and a minority defends Paul's authorship of all three letters.

events.intro: The letter presupposes Paul imprisoned in Rome, already after a first hearing, and awaiting condemnation. If it is his, it is from the last years of Nero; if it is by a disciple, it is some decades later. The dates are approximate.

context: The letter places Paul in Rome (1:17), imprisoned in chains and without the relative freedom of the rented house described at the end of Acts. The Christians of the city had suffered Nero's violence after the fire of 64, and ancient tradition, from Clement of Rome (c. 96) on, speaks of the deaths of Peter and Paul in the capital. Timothy, for his part, seems to be in Asia, probably in Ephesus, in a region where many had deserted Paul (1:15). The text reflects a generation of transition: the founders are disappearing, and the concern is that the teaching received pass to “faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well” (2:2).
